narrative_idea_gen: Told through the drifting, associative consciousness of Maureen Kettleworth—perpetual third alternate and unofficial archivist of the Dunnhaven Ladies' Curling Club—this sprawling comedic epic chronicles the club's improbable forty-year journey from a neglected Scottish village league to the 2019 World Senior Championships, dwelling in the sacred micro-rituals of post-match tea rotation, the unspoken politics of who drives the minibus, and the way Janet's shortbread tin materializes at precisely the worst emotional junctures. The great invisible engine of their rise is that not a single woman on the five-person roster actually wants to keep advancing—each privately dreads the next qualifier but assumes she'd devastate the others by saying so—and so they keep winning with clenched smiles and roiling stomachs, their collective silence read by the sporting press as iron resolve. Maureen, who notices everything precisely because she is never quite on the ice, watches their legendary unbeaten streak finally shatter in a catastrophic semifinal, and registers on each teammate's face not grief but a relief so naked it borders on ecstasy—only to then chronicle, in her meandering and deeply felt way, the repossession of the clubhouse, the evaporation of sponsors, the village's pivoting indifference, understanding at last that the loss was the single honest moment they ever shared, and that even honesty, arriving forty years late, saves nothing except the particular taste of Janet's shortbread on a bus ride home no one will remember correctly.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Scene-Level Beats for the Dunnhaven Ladies' Curling Club Story

---

## Beat 1: The Third Alternate's Confession of Peripheral Omniscience

**Concrete Action:** Maureen Kettleworth introduces herself not by name but by function — or rather, by the absence of function. She is the perpetual third alternate. She has never delivered a stone in competitive play. She has, however, kept every scorecard, laundered every team jersey, and memorized the precise order in which each woman takes her tea. She tells us, in her wandering way, that the Dunnhaven Ladies' Curling Club reached the 2019 World Senior Championships. She tells us they lost. Then, almost parenthetically, buried in a subordinate clause about the quality of the arena coffee in Stavanger, she tells us something else: every single one of them was glad.

**Narrative Technique:** *Peripatetic first-person disclosure from the designated marginal witness.* Maureen's associative drift — the way she can't mention the semifinal without veering into the coffee, the coffee without veering into Janet's opinion of Continental biscuits, Janet's opinion without doubling back to 1979 — is not a tic but the story's primary instrument. Like Cortázar's narrator announcing "Now I am an axolotl" on page one, Maureen surrenders the emotional payload early: *they were relieved.* But the confession arrives swaddled in so many digressions that the reader may not immediately register its enormity. The story's task is to make us feel, retroactively, what we were told prospectively. The structural wager is identical to "Axolotl" — reveal the ending, then make the reader *understand* it — but the method is inverted: where Cortázar's narrator is eerily direct, Maureen buries the truth in the texture of everything else, which is its own kind of honesty.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The comedy of a woman who has spent forty years on the bench describing herself as if this were the most natural observational post in the world. "You see more from where I sit, which is to say, from where I've always sat, which is just there, behind the barrier, next to the bag with the knee braces." Her lack of self-pity is what makes the position devastating. She has organized her entire identity around noticing, and what she has noticed — for four decades — is a lie everyone was telling with their bodies.

**Why It Works:** The third alternate is the ideal narrator for a story about collective self-deception because she is *of* the group but never *in* the action. She has all the emotional proximity and none of the performative pressure. She can see their faces in the moments between stones, when the crowd noise fades and a woman's expression resets before anyone notices. The choice to frame the story through Maureen means that the reader inherits her vantage: close enough to love these women, far enough to see what they refuse to see in each other. The structural function is to establish that this is a story narrated by someone who knows the ending before the beginning, who has always known, and whose tragedy is not ignorance but the inability to intervene. She is an archive, not an actor. Archives don't save anyone; they just remember.

---

## Beat 2: The Origin as Accident — The First Match No One Meant to Win

**Concrete Action:** Maureen recounts how the club began. It was 1979. Five women in Dunnhaven needed something to do on Thursday evenings that was not their houses. The village had an old curling rink with dodgy ice and a roof that leaked when it was warm enough for the ice to be bad and cold enough for the roof to matter. They entered the regional league because the entry form was pinned to the noticeboard at the post office and Phyllis Taggart mistook it for a community social signup. They won their first match because the opposing team from Kirkhallam fielded only three players (a stomach flu) and seemed confused about the direction of play. They won their second match because Janet, who had never held a curling stone, released her first competitive delivery so badly that it removed three of the opposition's stones in a configuration that the skip from Blairgowrie later called "physically improbable." Nobody celebrated. Phyllis asked if they could stop at the chippy on the way home.

**Narrative Technique:** *Comic anti-genesis — the mythic origin revealed as a series of administrative errors and gastrointestinal misfortunes.* Where the "Axolotl" narrator drifts to the aquarium through aimless boredom, the Dunnhaven women drift into competitive curling through a stapled flyer and a misunderstanding. The deflected causality is the same — Cortázar's "wrong path through the garden" becomes Maureen's "Phyllis couldn't read the fine print without her other glasses" — but the register is comic rather than uncanny. The deeper resonance, however, is identical: something enormous begins for no good reason. The absence of intention at the origin is what makes the forty-year entrapment so poignant; there was never a moment of *choosing* this, which means there was never a clean moment to un-choose it.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The detail of Janet's first stone — the physically improbable shot that becomes, in Maureen's telling, both the club's founding miracle and its original curse. Every great run has an origin myth; Maureen gives us one that is simultaneously ridiculous and, in retrospect, ominous. The chippy on the way home establishes the bus/car ride as a recurring structural unit — the journey between the rink and the rest of their lives, where the real emotional processing happens, mediated by food.

**Why It Works:** The thematic engine of the story — that these women never wanted what they achieved — must be established at the root. By making the origin accidental, Maureen shows us that the silence began before anyone had anything to be silent about. The club was never about ambition. It was about Thursday evenings and not being in one's house. Every subsequent victory is a further departure from the original impulse, and the women's inability to say "this has gone far enough" is not cowardice but a form of loyalty to each other: each assumes the others want this, and no one can bear to be the one who takes it away. The structural function is to plant the seed of the central irony in the soil of comedy so that it grows into something much darker over the next four decades without ever losing its absurd roots.

---

## Beat 3: The Forty-Year Compression — Iterative Narration of Ritual, Victory, and Unspoken Dread

**Concrete Action:** Maureen collapses decades into recurring patterns. The qualification rounds blur. The regional championships blur. What remains sharply individuated are the micro-rituals: the rotation of who makes tea and in what order (a system of baroque complexity that encodes hierarchies no one will name); the politics of the minibus (who drives, who rides shotgun, who controls the radio, what happens when Phyllis and Janet are not speaking and must be separated by at least one row of seats); the shortbread tin (Janet's, always Janet's, materializing at funerals, after arguments, during rain delays, offered without comment and accepted without thanks, a eucharist of butter and flour). Intercut with these rituals — which Maureen renders with the devotional precision of a medieval chronicler — are flashes of the ascent: the county championship in 1986, the national ranking in 1994, the first newspaper clipping (which Maureen laminated and which now lives in a shoebox in her hall cupboard). The unbeaten streak begins somewhere in here, though no one remembers exactly when, because it accrued the same way a stalactite accrues — drip by drip, in the dark, and by the time you notice it, it's a geological feature.

**Narrative Technique:** *Frequentative narration laced with the singular — Genette's iterative mode shot through with irreducible specifics.* Like the "Axolotl" narrator's compressed daily visits, Maureen's account of forty years operates primarily in the tense of "every time" and "always" and "Phyllis would invariably" — but punctuated by the singular: a specific argument in a specific car park in 1991, the exact time the bus broke down outside Perth (4:17 PM, a Tuesday, because of course Maureen remembers). The technique simultaneously conveys the numbing accumulation of years and preserves the fierce particularity of individual moments. The reader experiences both: the long blur and the bright stab.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The digressions *are* the content. Maureen's account of the tea rotation is not a tangent from the story of the championships; it *is* the story of the championships, because the real drama was never on the ice. It was always in the small negotiations of proximity and care between five women who spent more waking hours together than with their families. The shortbread tin as emotional barometer — appearing "at precisely the worst emotional junctures" — becomes the story's equivalent of Cortázar's aquarium glass: an ordinary object that, through sheer repetitive presence, becomes sacred.

**Why It Works:** Structural compression of forty years is the only way to convey the particular horror of a slow-motion entrapment that never had a single decisive moment. No one woman woke up one morning and chose silence; the silence was *iterative,* built from a thousand small non-conversations. By rendering the ascent as ritual rather than drama, Maureen shows us that the club's "iron resolve" — as the press reads it — was actually the iron resolve of British social decorum: no one mentioning the elephant because the elephant has been in the room so long it has its own seat assignment on the minibus. The structural function is to build pressure. Forty years of compressed ritual must make the reader feel both the comfort of these patterns and their suffocating weight, so that when the loss finally comes, we understand — in our bodies, not just our minds — why relief is the only possible response.

---

## Beat 4: The Phenomenology of Not-Wanting — Maureen's Portrait of Five Women Trapped by Courtesy

**Concrete Action:** Maureen pauses the forward momentum of the timeline to do what she does best: look closely. She gives us each woman in turn — not a biography but a *reading.* Phyllis, who captains the team with the grim efficiency of someone organizing a school fête that has spiraled beyond all reasonable scale. Janet, whose shortbread production has increased in direct proportion to her anxiety, and who now bakes three tins before each match — one for the team, one for the officials, one "just in case," the "just in case" covering a category of emotional emergency Janet will never articulate. Eileen, who has twice written letters of resignation and twice used them as bookmarks. Dot, who privately suspects she has been curling with a torn rotator cuff since 2003 but will not see a doctor because diagnosis would become an excuse and an excuse would become a betrayal. And through it all, Maureen herself — who suspects, who more than suspects, who *knows* — but whose role as third alternate has trained her in the discipline of standing behind the barrier and not intervening.

**Narrative Technique:** *Comic ekphrasis of emotional concealment — each woman rendered as a still life of suppression.* Where Cortázar's narrator describes the axolotl's golden eyes as windows onto trapped consciousness, Maureen describes Janet's hands crimping shortbread as windows onto trapped dread. The technique is the same: lavish, obsessive attention to physical detail that keeps tipping from observation into interpretation, from the visible into the inferred. The comedy comes from the gap between the women's surfaces — competent, stoic, Scottish — and the roiling interiors Maureen maps with the confidence of someone who has been reading these faces for longer than some marriages last.

**What Makes It Memorable:** Eileen's resignation letters used as bookmarks. Dot's undiagnosed shoulder. These are not broad comedic strokes; they are small, specific, deeply human acts of self-erasure performed in the name of not letting the others down. The reader laughs and then stops laughing. Cortázar made us see consciousness in axolotl eyes; Maureen makes us see desperation in shortbread. Both rely on the narrator's willingness to look longer than is comfortable.

**Why It Works:** This beat is the story's philosophical core, its equivalent of "Axolotl"'s "they were not animals." The central recognition — that five women have been performing enthusiasm for four decades because each believes she owes it to the other four — is the engine of both the comedy and the tragedy. The structural function is to slow time to a near-standstill and force the reader to sit with these portraits, the way Maureen has sat with these women. We must *see* them clearly before the loss, so that when the loss comes and their faces finally match their feelings, the reader understands exactly what is being released. This is also the beat where Maureen's position as archivist becomes most clearly a form of love and most clearly a form of paralysis. She has catalogued their suffering with exquisite care. She has helped no one.

---

## Beat 5: The Sporting Press and the Mythology of Resolve — The Lie Seen from Outside

**Concrete Action:** Maureen describes, with a mixture of bemusement and something rawer, the way the outside world has narrated the Dunnhaven Ladies' Curling Club. The sporting press picks them up sometime in the mid-2000s. The unbeaten streak gets a name. Feature articles appear. The phrases are always the same: "steely determination," "quiet professionalism," "the spirit of Scottish grit." A BBC Scotland documentary crew spends two days with them in 2016. Maureen watches the finished film, in which Phyllis's tight-lipped refusal to discuss strategy is interpreted as competitive secrecy, Janet's constant baking is framed as "team bonding through tradition," and Dot's visible wince when she lifts a stone is narrated as "playing through pain — the hallmark of a champion." The documentary does not interview Maureen. She is visible in three shots, slightly out of focus, holding a clipboard.

**Narrative Technique:** *Ironic counternarrative — the external mythology placed in direct, unresolved tension with Maureen's internal knowledge.* This beat functions like a mirror held at the wrong angle: everything the press says is technically true and completely false. Cortázar's story asks "what happens when you look at the Other so hard you become it"; this beat asks "what happens when others look at you so carelessly they invent you entirely." The press's language — iron resolve, grit, pain tolerance — is the exact inverse of the truth Maureen has shown us. The structural irony is excruciating and very funny. The women cannot correct the record without destroying the team
narrative_story:
# The Dunnhaven Ladies' Curling Club

---

I should say first that I am the third alternate, which means I am the woman who replaces the woman who replaces the woman who replaces one of the women who actually play. In forty years I have never delivered a stone in competitive play. I have held stones. I have carried stones. I have, on one occasion in 1997, warmed a stone against my body in a car park outside Dumfries because Eileen had read somewhere that temperature variation affects the curl and the boot of the minibus had a draft that came in through the rust, which itself came in through the salt, which was Phyllis's fault for storing road grit beside the equipment bag, though to be fair to Phyllis the grit was there because Janet had refused to let anyone track slush into the Dunfermline Travelodge and someone had to put it somewhere and Phyllis is, if nothing else, a woman who solves problems by absorbing them into her personal vicinity, which is how she ended up captaining the team in the first place, and also how she ended up with sciatica, two storage units, and a freezer full of casseroles she made for other people's crises and then forgot to deliver.

My name is Maureen Kettleworth. I keep the scorecards. I launder the jerseys. I know that Phyllis takes her tea with one sugar and a splash of milk added *after* the sugar has dissolved, not before, and that this distinction matters to Phyllis in a way she will never explain but which I suspect has something to do with her mother, because everything about Phyllis that cannot be explained by logic can be explained by her mother, who was a tremendous woman in the way that a weather system is tremendous, meaning you survived her or you didn't, and Phyllis survived her, barely, and has spent the rest of her life making sure every small thing is done in the right order as if order itself could be a form of shelter.

I know that Janet takes hers black. I know that Eileen won't drink tea at all before a match but will drink precisely half a cup afterward, and that if you fill it past the halfway mark she will stare at it with the expression of someone who has been personally affronted by crockery. I know that Dot takes three sugars and has been told by her GP to take none and so takes two when Phyllis is watching and three when she isn't, and I know this because I am always watching, which is what happens when you spend forty years on a bench behind a barrier next to the bag with the knee braces.

You see more from where I sit, which is to say, from where I've always sat, which is just there, behind the barrier, next to the bag with the knee braces. The knee braces are mine. Well—some of them are mine. The beige elastic one with the metal stays is Dot's, and the neoprene sleeve is Janet's, though Janet insists she's never worn it and it must belong to someone else, meaning it belongs to Janet, because Janet is the only person I've ever met who lies exclusively about her own joints.

I should tell you what happened. The Dunnhaven Ladies' Curling Club reached the semifinal of the 2019 World Senior Curling Championships, which were held in Stavanger, Norway, where the arena had the kind of fluorescent lighting that makes everyone look like they've already died and the coffee was served from a machine that produced a liquid bearing the same relationship to coffee that a photocopy of a painting bears to the painting, which is to say it was technically the same shape and contained some of the same information but was missing whatever quality makes you glad to be alive, and Janet said the biscuits were "Continental," by which she did not mean French or Italian or in any way sophisticated but meant, specifically, that they were flat, dry, and tasted of nothing, which is how Janet has used the word "Continental" since at least 1979 when she and Phyllis went on a coach tour of Belgium, a trip about which Janet has never volunteered a single positive detail and which, I believe, inoculated her permanently against anything that occurred east of the North Sea—and in the semifinal, in that arena, under those lights, with that coffee, the Dunnhaven Ladies' Curling Club lost.

They lost to the Swedish national team, 7-3, in eight ends.

And every single one of them was glad.

---

It started, as these things do, because of a leaflet. Or rather it started because Phyllis Taggart could not find her reading glasses—her *other* reading glasses, the ones she kept in her handbag rather than on the chain around her neck, the chain being reserved for what she called her "official" glasses, which she wore for driving, church, and arguing with the council, the handbag pair being for everything else, meaning everything that Phyllis considered to be occurring in a lower register of formality—and without them, the notice pinned to the board in the Dunnhaven post office was nothing more than a promising blur.

What Phyllis saw, or believed she saw, was a signup sheet for a community social evening at the ice rink. What it actually was, was an entry form for the 1979-80 East Central Scotland Ladies' Curling League, Division Four.

This was 1979. Phyllis was forty-one. Janet was thirty-nine. Eileen was thirty-seven and newly separated from Gordon, which no one spoke about directly but which had settled over the village like weather, everyone adjusting their indoor arrangements accordingly. Dot was forty-three and had just been made redundant from the woolen mill. I was thirty-six and lived alone and had always lived alone and would continue to live alone, which I mention not for sympathy—I have never wanted sympathy; sympathy requires a wound, and the absence of certain things is not a wound but a topography, a way the land happens to lie—but because it explains why Phyllis's phone call found me at home on a Tuesday evening with nothing in particular to refuse.

"Thursday," Phyllis said. "The rink. It'll be a social. Bring something."

I brought shortbread, which turned out to be a mistake, because Janet also brought shortbread, and this was my first encounter with a fact that would govern the next four decades of my life: there is room in the Dunnhaven Ladies' Curling Club for only one shortbread, and it is Janet's. My tin was eaten. It was never mentioned again. I learned my place. I have since brought only cling film, plasters, and a thermos of tea with the correct number of sugars for each woman pre-dissolved in individual portions, which I keep in labelled jars in a small insulated bag, and about which no one has ever commented, not once, in forty years, which is either a compliment or an indictment and I have chosen to receive it as the former because the alternative would require a bitterness I do not have the energy to maintain.

The rink was not much. A low breeze-block building on the Kirkhallam road with a corrugated roof that leaked when it rained, which in that part of Scotland meant it leaked. The ice was maintained by a man called Angus Breck who also maintained the village cricket pitch in summer, which tells you everything you need to know about the quality of both surfaces. The changing rooms smelled of damp and ancient rubber and there was a hand-written sign above the door that said MIND YOUR HEAD, the final D partially obscured by a piece of tape on which someone had written, in different handwriting, SERIOUSLY.

We arrived on a Thursday evening. It was not a social. It was the first round of the East Central Division Four League. Our opponents were Kirkhallam B.

Phyllis, who had by now found her other glasses and read the entry form and understood the situation, said nothing. Phyllis is a woman for whom backing down from a public commitment, even a commitment entered into by accident, even a commitment entered into by optometric failure, is not possible. I have watched her eat an entire plate of kidneys at a Burns Night supper because she'd told the hostess she loved offal—this was a lie; Phyllis does not love offal; Phyllis does not *like* offal; Phyllis, I believe, regards offal with the same cold suspicion most people reserve for foreign policy—but she'd said it and so she ate it, every piece, chewing steadily, the way you might chew through a moral obligation. She showed up at the rink with her stones and her brush and her team of bewildered women and she said, "Right then."

Kirkhallam B fielded three players. A stomach flu had taken their lead and their second, and their skip, a tall woman named Morag whose expression suggested that the flu was the latest in a long sequence of personal betrayals, spent much of the match delivering stones with one hand while clutching her abdomen with the other. Their remaining player, whose name I never learned but who wore glasses thicker than mine, appeared uncertain about which end of the rink they were meant to be aiming for and at one point swept vigorously in the wrong direction.

We won.

Janet's first competitive delivery—her first ever, because she had never held a curling stone before that evening, or indeed expressed any interest in curling, or in sport, or in activity of any kind that could not be performed while seated near a kettle—left her hand at an angle that I can only describe as diagonal to intention. The stone traveled. It did not travel where Janet had aimed it, though where Janet had aimed it was itself unclear, since her delivery stance resembled someone trying to return a borrowed suitcase to a shelf slightly too high to reach. The stone crossed the ice in a wide, grieving arc, struck the first of Kirkhallam's placed stones at its outer edge, which redirected it into a second stone, which nudged a third, and when everything stopped moving three opposing stones had been removed from the house and Janet's stone sat alone in the centre, perfectly placed, spinning gently, as if it had always meant to be there.

Morag from Kirkhallam stared at the ice for a long time. Then she stared at Janet. Then she was sick in a bin.

Nobody celebrated. Phyllis asked if we could stop at the chippy on the way home. We could. We did. I had a fish supper and sat in the back of Phyllis's Cortina and the windows steamed up and we ate in near-silence except for Eileen, who said, "That was all right, actually," and Dot, who said, "My knees are going to regret this," and Phyllis, who said nothing but who, I noticed—because I am always noticing, because noticing is what I do instead of the other things people do—was sitting very still with a chip in her hand and a look on her face, and the look was not triumph and was not embarrassment but was something more complicated, something I didn't have a word for then but which I would learn, over the next four decades, to recognize in all of them, in different light, at different angles, a look that meant: *this is not my life, and yet here I am in it, and it is not altogether terrible.*

We had a team. We had not meant to have a team. Nobody had asked for one. The leaflet was wrong and Phyllis's glasses were wrong and Janet's delivery was—by any biomechanical standard—wrong, and none of it mattered because the thing about a wrong turn is that it takes you somewhere, and somewhere is different from where you were, and where we all were, in 1979, on Thursday evenings, was in our houses, and our houses were—

Well. Maureen, stop. That's not your story to tell. The houses were their own. The houses were fine. The houses were simply places that five women needed, on Thursdays, not to be.

---

The years did what years do, which is to say they accrued.

Every Thursday. Every Thursday the five of them—or four, officially, and me behind the barrier—would arrive at the rink and something would happen on the ice and something else, something different and more true, would happen in the spaces between the ice: in the changing room, in the car park, in the back of whichever vehicle was ferrying us to whichever draughty hall in whichever village had the misfortune of hosting that week's fixture.

I could tell you about the matches. I could tell you that we won the East Central Division Four title in 1980 and the Division Three title in 1982 and that Phyllis was nominated for the Regional Skip of the Year in 1984, an award she did not win but which came with a certificate that she kept in a drawer beneath her tea towels, neither displayed nor discarded, existing in the liminal state Phyllis reserves for compliments. I could tell you about the county championship in 1986—held in a rink in Forfar where the radiators were so powerful that the ice developed a thin film of melt by the fourth end and all the stones ran long and Dot said it was like playing curling in a bath—and I could tell you about the national ranking in 1994 and the special mention in the Scottish Curling Association's annual report, which used the phrase "remarkable consistency" in a way that could have meant either "they are very good" or "they have been doing this for a bewilderingly long time," and knowing the Scottish Curling Association, it meant both.

But that is not what I remember. What I remember—what is sharp, what is individuated, what rises from the long blur with the clarity of something that has happened not once but is happening still—is who made the tea.

The tea rotation was Phyllis's invention, which marks it as simultaneously logical and unassailable. The system was this: on ordinary practice nights, the person who had arrived first made the tea. On match days, the person who had played worst in the previous match made the tea, unless that person was Janet, in which case Eileen made it, because Janet's response to having played badly was to produce shortbread, and you could not have one woman performing two catering functions simultaneously without undermining the entire domestic economy of the team. On days when there had been an argument—and there were arguments; of course there were arguments; five women in close proximity for forty years generate arguments the way a river generates silt, slowly, continuously, depositing layers of grievance that harden into the landscape—on those days, the tea was made by the person who was *not* involved in the argument, which was almost always me, so in practice I made the tea after arguments, which means, in practice, I made a great deal of tea.

There was also the matter of the minibus.

The minibus came later—1990, I think, or 1991, because it was the year Dot's car failed its MOT and Eileen refused to drive any vehicle manufactured before 1985 on the grounds that pre-1985 seatbelts were "decorative." Phyllis drove. Phyllis always drove. This was not discussed; it was *understood,* the way plate tectonics are understood, as a fundamental condition of the earth. Janet rode shotgun, except when she and Phyllis were not speaking, in which case Janet sat in the second row and Eileen sat in the front and the radio was turned to Radio 2 rather than Radio 4, because Radio 4 was Phyllis's preference and Janet's silent exile from the front seat required a corresponding exile from the airwaves, a punishment so precise in its pettiness that I rather admired it, though I would never have said so, because the third alternate does not have opinions about seating arrangements any more than the furniture has opinions about the room.

When Janet and Phyllis were not speaking, Dot sat in the third row with me. Dot would say, "How long this time, do you think?" and I would say, "Hard to say," and Dot would say, "Shortbread by Wednesday," and she was always right. The shortbread was always the ceasefire. It would appear—Janet's tin, the blue one with the Highland cattle on the lid, which she'd had since at least 1983 and which had achieved, through sheer repetition of service, the status of a regimental colour—and it would be offered without comment. Phyllis would take a piece. She would eat it. She would not say thank you, because to say thank you would be to acknowledge that the shortbread was a gesture, and to acknowledge the gesture would be to acknowledge the argument, and to acknowledge the argument would be to introduce into their relationship the catastrophic possibility that things between them could be, and had been, wrong. So Phyllis would eat her shortbread and Janet would close the tin and the minibus would continue to its destination and the radio would return to Radio 4 and the world would be, for the moment, re-established.

The shortbread appeared at other times. It appeared after Dot's mother died, in 1995, offered in the car park of the crematorium without a word. It appeared when Eileen's son moved to Australia, and again six months later when he didn't come back for Christmas, and again the following year when he did

The Morska Conspiracy
The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door.

Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards.

Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood.
